summary: First English narrative for the Essex destination decision of November 1820, written from the case's structured facts.

narrative.hook: Your ship is gone, sunk by a whale, and you are standing in an open boat with twenty men and whatever you managed to throw into it. One heading is close and downwind; the other is more than twice as far, straight into the wind, and the only thing recommending it is that nobody has told you a frightening story about it.
narrative.short_setup: On November 20, 1820, a sperm whale rammed the Nantucket whaleship Essex twice and sank her in the middle of the South Pacific, roughly 2,000 nautical miles west of South America. Twenty survivors got away in three open whaleboats about twenty-five feet long, carrying salvaged hardtack, water, a few Galapagos tortoises and the navigational instruments they could grab. Over the next day or two, before the boats got underway, Captain George Pollard Jr. had to fix a destination. The Marquesas and Society Islands lay some 1,200 to 1,500 miles west-southwest, two or three weeks off with the trade winds behind them. The South American coast lay more than 3,000 miles east, against those same winds, reachable only by running south first in the hope of finding westerlies. There would be no resupply either way beyond rain and whatever fish they could catch.
narrative.why_option_a_made_sense: The case for the nearer islands was arithmetic the officers could do in their heads. A two-to-three-week downwind run demanded a fraction of the food and water that a multi-thousand-mile beat to windward would, and every day shaved off the passage was a day fewer of exposure in an undecked boat. Whaleboats were built for short chases, not ocean crossings; the less ocean they had to cross, the better the odds that boats, gear and men held together. The danger on that heading was of a different kind entirely — not running out of anything, but what might be waiting on the beach. And that danger, whatever its size, applied only at the end of a passage the boats could actually complete.
narrative.why_option_b_made_sense: The case for South America was that it pointed at a known world. The crew expected a populated, non-hostile coast, and the run east crossed shipping lanes where another whaler or trader might pick them up long before landfall — a second chance the empty western ocean did not offer. Against that, the fear of the islands was not idle superstition: cannibalism had genuinely been recorded among some Pacific island peoples by earlier European visitors, and the Essex's officers had no way at sea to check whether it applied to the particular islands ahead of them. Set against a specific, vividly imagined death, a longer hungry voyage looked like the familiar hazard. Whalemen had gone short on rations before and come through it.
narrative.actual_decision_explanation: Pollard's own instinct was for the nearer islands. His two mates, Owen Chase and Matthew Joy, argued him out of it, and he deferred. The stated reason was the one Pollard himself gave afterward: the crew feared being devoured by cannibals. The boats turned south and east for South America. It is worth being precise about what kind of knowledge that fear rested on — secondhand rumor and outdated or garbled reports from earlier voyagers, not anything the officers had seen or could verify about the islands in question. It is also worth noting that the two surviving first-hand accounts, Chase's published narrative and Thomas Nickerson's manuscript written decades later, differ somewhat on how hard Pollard pressed his own preference before giving way.
narrative.outcome_story: The three boats were separated during the voyage and one was never found. Food and water gave out weeks before any coast appeared. Men died of starvation and exposure, and the survivors ate the bodies of the dead. On Pollard's boat the crew eventually drew lots; the lot fell to Owen Coffin, Pollard's own first cousin, who was shot by Charles Ramsdell and eaten. Three men who had chosen to stay behind on uninhabited Henderson Island lived there on birds, eggs and shellfish until they were taken off. Of the twenty who left the wreck, eight survived: three from Chase's boat, picked up on February 18, 1821 off the coast of Chile; two from Pollard's, on February 23; and the three from Henderson Island on April 9. Chase published his account later that year, and it is understood to have influenced Melville's Moby-Dick.
narrative.hindsight_analysis: The outcome was about as bad as an outcome gets, but the outcome is not the argument. What makes this decision weak is visible without knowing how it ended: the two risks being weighed were not the same kind of thing, and the officers had the means to notice. Distance, prevailing winds and the provisions in the boats were quantities they worked with professionally; a supply shortfall over 3,000 miles of windward sailing was calculable in fairly concrete terms. The cannibal risk was a rumor about places they had never been, with no way to check it and no estimate of its size. Trading a measurable hazard for an unmeasurable one is a poor trade even when it happens to work out, and the fact that Pollard, the most experienced man aboard, initially leaned the other way suggests the better reading was available in the room. What hindsight should not do is overclaim the counterfactual. We know the three men on Henderson Island came to no harm; we do not know what would have met twenty men landing on the Marquesas or the Societies. The islands route was very likely survivable, but 'very likely' is an inference drawn afterward, not a fact the crew withheld from themselves. The honest verdict is narrower and harder: they chose the risk they could feel over the risk they could count, and the risk they could count was the one that killed twelve of them.
narrative.decision_principle: When a vivid, unmeasurable danger is weighed against a dull, calculable one, the calculable one tends to lose — not because it is smaller, but because it is harder to feel. Before trading them, ask which of the two you could actually put a number on, and why the other one is winning anyway.
narrative.longform_story:
The whaleship Essex was 2,000 miles west of South America and nearly three months out of the Galapagos when, on November 20, 1820, a large sperm whale struck her twice and opened the hull. She went down fast enough that the crew's work was less salvage than scramble: hardtack, casks of water, a few Galapagos tortoises still alive in the hold, a compass, a quadrant, some navigation books. Twenty men got clear in three whaleboats — open, undecked craft about twenty-five feet long, built to chase whales for a few hours and return to a ship that no longer existed.

The decision that followed took a day or two and would kill most of them. It was, in outline, simple. West-southwest, roughly 1,200 to 1,500 miles off, lay the Marquesas and the Society Islands. The trade winds and the currents both ran that way; two to three weeks, by the officers' own estimate. East lay South America, more than 3,000 miles distant, and the same trades that would push them to the islands stood squarely in the way of getting there. The eastern route meant running far south first, hoping to pick up westerlies at a higher latitude, then turning. Either way there would be no resupply. Rain, fish, and what was already in the boats.

Pollard, the captain, wanted the islands. Chase and Joy, his first and second mates, did not, and the reason they gave was cannibals. Pollard, recalling it later, put it plainly: the crew feared being devoured. He let himself be talked around.

It is easy to file that under superstition and move on, and it would be wrong. Cannibalism among some Pacific island peoples was not a sailors' invention — it had been recorded by earlier European visitors, in Fiji and in parts of the Marquesas among others. What the Essex's officers had was not a fantasy but a real category of risk applied to the wrong level of precision: general reports, secondhand and years stale, stretched over specific islands none of them had visited. By 1820 American and European ships had in fact called at the Marquesas and the Societies repeatedly without incident. There was simply no way to establish that from an open boat in the middle of the ocean. The information the crew needed existed; it was just not available to them.

So they weighed one thing they could not measure against another they could. Distance, wind and rations were the working substance of their trade. Any whaling officer could reason about how long a boat could keep men alive over a given passage. Three thousand miles to windward against fifteen hundred downwind is not a close arithmetic question, and the answer does not depend on knowing the future. The eastern route asked for far more than the boats held, with almost no margin for a calm, a storm, or a navigational error. That was knowable on November 21.

What was not knowable was the shape of the disaster. The boats separated. One vanished entirely and was never accounted for. On the other two the food ran out, then the water, and then men began to die. The survivors ate them — first the dead, as a grim necessity that whalemen of the period understood as the last extremity of shipwreck, and finally, in Pollard's boat, not the dead. They drew lots. The lot fell to Owen Coffin, seventeen years old and Pollard's first cousin, whose mother had placed him in the captain's care. Charles Ramsdell shot him.

Three men had already peeled off from this. When the boats touched at Henderson Island — uninhabited, with a thin supply of birds, eggs and shellfish and almost no fresh water — they chose to take their chances ashore rather than continue. All three lived. They were taken off on April 9, 1821. The others reached rescue at sea: three from Chase's boat on February 18 off Chile, two from Pollard's on February 23. Eight of twenty.

The irony writes itself, and that is exactly the reason to be careful with it. The danger they fled never touched the men who stopped on an island; the safety they sailed toward consumed the rest. But the three on Henderson were not on the Marquesas, and twenty starving men making landfall is not three. What the case actually demonstrates is narrower and more useful than 'they feared the wrong thing.' It is that the two fears were not commensurable, and the officers did not notice they were comparing them as if they were. One risk came with numbers attached and a professional's ability to check them. The other came with a story. The story won.

Pollard's own hesitation is the detail that keeps this from being hindsight bias. The most experienced navigator in the boats leaned toward the islands first and was argued down by subordinates whose case rested on the weaker evidence. That is not a decision that only looks bad afterward. It looked answerable at the time, to at least one man present.

Owen Chase published his account of the wreck in 1821, and it found its way to a young Herman Melville, who would write his own whale. Nickerson, the fourteen-year-old cabin boy, wrote his version decades later; the manuscript surfaced only in the twentieth century, and the two accounts do not perfectly agree about who pushed hardest in the debate that settled everything. On the substance of the choice, though, they agree. The boats turned east, into more ocean than they could carry.
